request: We need an app for staff to check attendees in at the venue entrance on the event day.

problem.value: Staff need to identify arriving attendees at the venue entrance and record their arrival on the event day. The underlying need (control access, count headcount, produce an attendance record, or all three) is not stated.
problem.evidence: Client: "We need an app for staff to check attendees in at the venue entrance on the event day."

current_process.value: Unknown how check-in is done today (paper list, spreadsheet, another tool, or no process).

existing_solutions.value: Unknown whether a registration or ticketing platform that already offers check-in is in use, whether an off-the-shelf event check-in app was considered, and what budget applies. Buying or reusing could remove the build.

success_metrics.value: Presumed: no queue at the door, an accurate record of who came, and no failures on the day. Targets such as seconds per attendee are not defined.
success_metrics.evidence: Deduced from the event-operations context; not stated by the client.

payer.value: Assumed an internal or commissioned tool, so the requester pays. No product revenue model.
payer.evidence: The request is phrased as "we need an app", not a product idea.

actors.value: Staff scanning or searching at the entrance (the primary operator) and attendees arriving. Probably also an event manager watching the numbers. Unknown who owns the attendee list, who handles exceptions, and whether staff are trained or are temporary hostesses.

business_objects.value: Event, Attendee (with a category), Registration, Check-in, possibly Zone/Session and Badge. The origin of the attendee list is unknown (imported, from a registration system, or created in this app).

business_rules.value: Unknown: who may enter, whether categories (VIP, press, speaker) get different access, and what a second scan of the same person means (duplicate to block, re-entry to allow, or a different zone or session).

workflow.value: Presumed flow: attendee arrives, staff identify them (scan or name search), the app confirms they are expected, and arrival is recorded. Unknown: how identification fails over, walk-ins and on-the-spot registration, what happens after the event, and where the attendee list originates.
workflow.evidence: Client: "check attendees in at the venue entrance".

integrations.value: Unknown: the source of the attendee list (registration or ticketing tool, CRM, spreadsheet), whether it changes up to the event day, whether check-ins must flow back to another system, and whether anyone is notified (for example a host when a VIP arrives).

permissions.value: Presumed: staff can check in and look up attendees; a manager sees the live counts and exports. Attendee personal data should be visible to staff only as far as needed. Details unknown.
permissions.evidence: Deduced; GDPR on attendee data is noted in the context.

config_vs_custom.value: Unknown whether this is a throwaway app for one event or the first instance of a reusable kit for many events. This changes the data model, configuration and cost.

constraints.value: The event date is fixed and cannot move. Unknown: the date, the number of attendees and entrances, the devices staff will use, venue connectivity, and GDPR constraints on attendee data.
constraints.evidence: Client: "on the event day" (a fixed date implied).

edge_cases.value: Unknown handling of: no connectivity at the venue, a failed scan or misspelled name, people not on the list (walk-ins, substitutions), the same person at two doors within seconds, and badge-less arrivals.

reporting.value: Likely a live count of arrivals and a post-event attendance export. Format and consumers (client, sponsors, invoicing) are unknown.
reporting.evidence: Deduced; attendance data is typically a post-event deliverable.

acceptance.value: Not defined. Likely a rehearsal on real devices at the venue with a target time per attendee.

risks.value: Main risk is a queue at the door on a date that cannot move. A manual fallback (paper list) and a rehearsal should be part of the rollout.

acquisition.value: Not applicable: this is an internal rollout to a known set of staff on the event day.
acquisition.evidence: Request describes a tool for the requester's own staff.

questions.q: Do you already have a registration or ticketing tool (or an event app you license) that includes check-in, and have you looked at buying one? If so, what budget applies?
questions.why: Buying or switching on an existing feature could remove the build entirely, and the budget sizes everything else.

questions.q: Where does the list of expected attendees come from today, and does it keep changing right up to and during the event (walk-ins, substitutions, cancellations)?
questions.why: The upstream list is the app's core data. A frozen import versus a live, moving list are very different builds.

questions.q: Will the venue entrance have reliable internet? Should check-in keep working if the connection drops?
questions.why: Working offline is an architecture decision (local copy of the list, syncing later). It is rarely stated but often assumed, and it is the most common cause of failure on the day.

questions.q: What does a second scan of the same person mean for you: block it as a duplicate, allow re-entry after stepping out, or record entry to a different zone or session? Do attendee categories (VIP, press, speaker) get different treatment?
questions.why: These are three different meanings with three different data models, and they decide what the app records.

questions.q: Is this for one event on a specific date, or should it be reusable for future events? What is the date, roughly how many attendees, and how many entrances?
questions.why: A throwaway app versus a reusable kit changes cost and design. Date and volume set the deadline and the required throughput at the door.

questions.q: How is check-in handled today, and what do you need afterwards (live counts, an attendance export, and for whom)?
questions.why: Establishes the baseline to improve on and whether the post-event attendance record is the real deliverable.

summary.scope: Likely scope: the attendee list, identification by scan or name search, recording arrival, and a live count with a post-event attendance export. Offline operation, a manual fallback, walk-in registration and multi-zone access are possible additions depending on the answers.

challenges.headline: Build versus use existing check-in
challenges.premise: A custom app has to be built for this event's check-in.
challenges.alternative: If attendees are already registered in a ticketing or registration tool, that tool's check-in feature, or a licensed event check-in app, could cover the door entirely. A custom build then only fills gaps, such as a specific export or a specific rule.
challenges.consequence: Building a custom app when check-in is already available or purchasable spends effort and adds failure risk on an immovable date, for no gain.
challenges.recommendation: Before any design, find out what registration or ticketing tool supplies the attendee list and whether it has a check-in feature or a priced add-on. Proceed to a build only if the gap is clearly stated.

challenges.headline: Assumed reliable venue connectivity
challenges.premise: The request implies the app can simply look up and record attendees live at the entrance.
challenges.alternative: Treat offline-capable check-in as the starting design question. A local copy of the list with later syncing keeps the door moving if the network drops. A thin online-only app with a paper-list fallback is a lower-cost alternative if the venue connection is proven.
challenges.consequence: An online-only build that meets a weak connection on the day produces a queue in front of the client, with no time to fix it. An offline build adds sync and conflict handling that costs more if it turns out not to be needed.
challenges.recommendation: Ask the venue about the real connection at each entrance, and test it on site, before choosing between the two designs.

challenges.headline: Check-in as a simple yes/no
challenges.premise: Checking someone in is a single arrival tick on a fixed list.
challenges.alternative: Decide up front what a second scan means (duplicate, re-entry, or entry to another zone or session) and whether attendee categories get different treatment. Also plan for walk-ins and substitutions as a normal path, not an exception.
challenges.consequence: A simple tick-box model has to be reworked once zones, re-entry or late additions show up, and it gives wrong attendance numbers in the meantime.
challenges.recommendation: Settle the second-scan meaning and the walk-in policy with the client before the data model is fixed.

an attendee list that keeps changing during the event
defined outcomes for the same person processed at two doors
peak throughput measured on real devices

Venue connectivity is unknown and may only be discoverable on site.
The source of the attendee list is unknown, so import or integration effort cannot be sized.
Staff may be temporary and untrained, so a confusing interface fails at peak arrival time.
Attendee personal data is held on staff devices, which brings GDPR obligations for access and for retention after the event.

opportunities.text: If more events are likely, design the attendee, category and check-in model as a reusable event kit rather than a one-off. Only do this once the client confirms there will be further events.
Make the check-in record, which carries who, when and where, the single source for the live count and the post-event attendance export.

next_steps: Find out which registration or ticketing tool holds the attendee list and whether it already offers check-in or a priced add-on. Decide build or buy before anything else.
Confirm the event date, attendee count, number of entrances, devices and venue connectivity, then choose between offline-capable and online-only.
Agree with the client what a second scan means, how categories are treated, and how walk-ins are handled, and define a target time per attendee.
If building, plan a rehearsal on real devices at the venue and a paper-list fallback as part of the delivery.

briefs.problem: Staff need to identify arriving attendees at the door and record their arrival quickly and reliably on a date that cannot move; the purpose behind it (queue control, headcount, attendance data) is assumed, not stated.
briefs.solution: A simple, one-handed check-in app for on-site staff: an attendee list on their devices, identification by scan or name search, an arrival record, a manual fallback for every failed scan, and a live count with post-event export (proposed, not yet confirmed).
introduces: a local attendee snapshot on staff devices with later sync, if offline use is needed
a check-in event record that separates duplicate, re-entry and other-zone arrivals
multi-device concurrency handling across several entrances
on-the-spot registration and fuzzy name search for walk-ins and failed scans

challenges.headline: Building instead of reusing
challenges.premise: A custom app is needed for check-in.
challenges.alternative: If the attendees already sit in a registration or ticketing tool, that tool may have a check-in feature that is already paid for or can be switched on. A dedicated off-the-shelf event check-in product is another route. Either could remove most of the build for a one-day need.
challenges.consequence: Building a custom app means funding offline sync, concurrency, fallbacks and a rehearsal for a few hours of use. If an existing tool does the job, that is mostly wasted effort and carries day-of risk a proven product would not.
challenges.recommendation: Before any design, find out what registration or ticketing tool supplies the list, whether it has a check-in feature, and what budget exists. Build only if something concrete (a rule, a data need, an integration) rules the existing options out.

challenges.headline: Unstated connectivity assumption
challenges.premise: Staff will always have a network at the entrance, so a simple online app is enough.
challenges.alternative: Settle explicitly whether check-in must work with no connection. An offline-capable design holds a local copy of the list and syncs later. An online-only design is simpler but fails in a basement or on saturated wifi. Testing signal at the actual entrances is a cheap way to decide.
challenges.consequence: Assuming online and discovering on the day that the network drops stops the door in front of the client. Assuming offline without need pays for sync and conflict rules that were not required.
challenges.recommendation: Ask the venue about connectivity and test signal at the entrances. Treat offline as a day-one architecture decision rather than a late add-on.

challenges.headline: Check-in as a single action
challenges.premise: Checking someone in is one simple event: they are either in or not.
challenges.alternative: Define up front whether a second scan is a duplicate to block, a re-entry to allow, or access to another zone or session to record separately. Alternatively, scope the first release to one entry per attendee and add zones later.
challenges.consequence: The three meanings need different data models. Choosing wrongly after build changes what counts as attendance and can corrupt the post-event numbers.
challenges.recommendation: Get the client to pick one meaning, with the behaviour for the same person scanned at two doors within seconds, before the data model is drawn.

risks: The network fails at the door on a date that cannot move, producing a queue in front of the client.
Two devices process the same attendee within seconds and the outcome is undefined, so counts or access become wrong.
Untrained staff meet the app for the first time that morning, and a UI that is not obvious slows the door.
Late list changes (walk-ins, substitutions, name corrections) have no on-site path and get edited by hand.
Attendee personal data is held on staff devices and exported, which brings GDPR obligations on storage, retention after the event and what sponsors may receive.

opportunities.text: Design the attendee, category and check-in model so it can be reused for later events, even if the first release is built for one event only. This only pays off if the client confirms further events.
Treat the attendance record as the client deliverable from day one, so the live count and the post-event export come from the same accurate check-in data.

next_steps: Find out what registration or ticketing tool holds the attendee list, whether it has a check-in feature, and what the budget is. Decide build or reuse before designing anything.
Confirm the event date, expected volume and busiest 20 minutes, number of entrances and staff, devices, and venue connectivity. Use these to decide online-only versus offline-capable.
Have the client decide what a second scan means (duplicate, re-entry or other zone), how people are identified, and what happens to walk-ins and failed scans.
If building, commit to a core loop of list import, scan or name search, check-in record and manual fallback, with a rehearsal on real devices in the venue before the date.

briefs.problem: Staff cannot quickly and reliably identify arriving attendees and record their arrival at the entrance on a fixed event day, without queues at the door.
briefs.solution: A simple, training-free check-in app for door staff: identify an attendee by scan or name search, record arrival, handle people not on the list, and yield an attendance record afterwards.
introduces: an attendee-list import and on-the-day amendment path (walk-ins, substitutions, corrections)
a check-in event record with defined duplicate / re-entry behaviour
device-side offline operation with a local list snapshot and later sync (if offline is required)
multi-device concurrency handling across several entrances
a manual fallback for identification (fuzzy name search, on-the-spot registration)
a post-event attendance export that serves as the client deliverable

challenges.headline: Build before checking what exists
challenges.premise: A bespoke app is needed for check-in at this event.
challenges.alternative: If the client already licenses a platform with a check-in surface, or an off-the-shelf event check-in tool fits one event, configuring or buying it could cover the need with no build. A short comparison against the stated door requirements settles it.
challenges.consequence: Building from scratch for a single dated event spends effort on offline sync, concurrency and rehearsal that an existing, already-proven tool may already provide, and adds a bespoke system to maintain.
challenges.recommendation: Before any design work, find out what the client already has or has considered, and what the budget is. Only proceed to build if those options fail a specific requirement.

challenges.headline: Online-only door assumption
challenges.premise: The app can assume a working connection at the entrance, since the request does not mention connectivity.
challenges.alternative: Treat offline operation as an explicit decision: either confirm and test the venue's connectivity, or build the app to hold a local copy of the attendee list and sync check-ins later.
challenges.consequence: An online-only build that loses signal produces a queue at the door in front of the client, with no second chance on the date. An offline build instead adds sync, conflict rules and a visible pending state, a materially larger build.
challenges.recommendation: Get a connectivity answer for the actual entrances, and decide offline versus online-only explicitly before estimating.

challenges.headline: Check-in as a single action
challenges.premise: Checking in is one simple event: a person is either in or not.
challenges.alternative: Define the second-scan outcomes up front: block as a duplicate, allow as re-entry, or record against another zone or session. The minimal option is one entrance, one check-in, with a warning on repeat scans.
challenges.consequence: If the client later needs re-entry or multiple zones, a boolean 'checked in' flag forces a data-model change close to the event date, and ambiguous double-scan behaviour is the first thing to cause friction at the door.
challenges.recommendation: Ask the client to choose the repeat-scan behaviour and whether zones or sessions exist, and model check-in as individual events from the start.

complexity_reasons: offline capability and sync are undecided and swing the build size
several devices at several entrances create concurrency questions
the attendee list keeps changing up to and on the event day
a fixed date requires a manual fallback and a rehearsal on real hardware
briefs.cost_driver: whether offline operation with sync is required
risks: A queue forms at the door if scanning or the network fails and no manual fallback exists.
Untrained staff see the app for the first time that morning, so any non-obvious flow slows the line.
The attendee list source and format are unknown, so import and ongoing changes may be harder than assumed.
Attendee personal data (GDPR) sits on staff devices, which needs limits on what is shown and retained after the event.
The date cannot move, so any scope not rehearsed on the real devices in the venue is at risk of failing on the day.

opportunities.text: Model check-in as individual timestamped events per attendee, zone and device from the start, so re-entry, zones and the post-event attendance report fall out of the same data.
If the client expects more events, build the check-in flow and attendee/category model as a reusable event kit, with branding, categories and export format configurable per event.

next_steps: Ask the client what they use today and what they already license or have considered, plus the budget, and compare any candidate against the door requirements before committing to a build.
Collect the facts that size the build: event date, attendee count, number of entrances, devices, venue connectivity, and where the attendee list comes from.
Get the client's decision on repeat-scan behaviour, walk-ins, and one event versus a reusable kit, then agree the success measures (seconds per attendee, live count, post-event list).
If building, plan around a minimal core flow with a manual fallback and a rehearsal on real devices in the venue, with other features only if they fit before the date.

decisions.decision: Attendees are identified by scan or name search, with a manual fallback for any scan path
decisions.why: Scanning can fail on the day, so identification must degrade gracefully rather than stop the line.
decisions.tradeoff: Extra build for search and on-the-spot registration, in exchange for not blocking the door when a scan fails.

decisions.decision: The requester is treated as the payer of a commissioned system for their own event, not a product to sell
The event date is fixed and scope is cut against it
decisions.why: The request ties the app to the event day.
decisions.alternative: Moving the date to fit the scope.
decisions.tradeoff: Features are dropped before the date is moved, so the core door flow must be finished and rehearsed first.
